claims.text: A hybrid method combining DFT-guided machine-learned interatomic potentials with Boltzmann transport analysis can separately model lattice and electronic thermal transport.
The proposed method can decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly accounting for atomic-scale disorder and defect scattering, including approximately 1 wt.% oxygen, enables this transport-channel decoupling.
The hybrid method will reduce conductivity-prediction error by approximately 20–30% relative to traditional perfect-crystal approaches.
HfNbTaTiZr should be modeled in both an ideal defect-free state and a disordered state containing roughly 1 wt.% oxygen.
Vacancies, substitutional disorder, and oxygen impurities alter local bonding environments and scattering mechanisms.
Static interatomic-length disorder and temperature-driven dynamic lattice distortion affect HEA structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties.
Explicit simulation of defect-induced lattice distortions and local-environment variations directly models the scattering events affecting phonon and electron transport.
Direct treatment of those scattering events makes the resulting Boltzmann transport calculations more accurate.
DFT electronic states coupled to a linearized Boltzmann transport equation can provide electronic conductivity and electronic thermal conductivity separately.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
From 300 to 1200 K, oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr has total thermal conductivity in the range 10–17 W/(K·m).
Existing analytical and simulation approaches generally assume perfect, defect-free bulk crystals.
Existing Debye-temperature-based approaches conflate lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
The proposed method should remain robust through 1200 K when defect characteristics, including oxygen contents up to 1 wt.%, are accurately represented.
Predictions may be less reliable above 1200 K or for unmodeled non-equilibrium states and excessive defect concentrations.
Electronic thermal conductivity can be inferred from electrical resistivity using the Wiedemann–Franz relation.
Failure to achieve approximately a 20–30% error improvement or failure to reproduce the stated low- and high-temperature trends would falsify the hypothesis.
